content: The use of tetracycline-class drugs during periods of tooth development, including the last half of pregnancy, infancy, and childhood up to the age of 8 years, can result in permanent discoloration of the teeth, ranging from yellow to gray-brown. This adverse effect is more frequently observed with prolonged use but has also been reported after repeated short-term courses. Enamel hypoplasia has also been documented. Consequently, tetracycline drugs should not be administered to this age group unless alternative treatments are ineffective or contraindicated. Tetracyclines form stable calcium complexes in bone-forming tissues. In premature infants receiving oral tetracycline at doses of 25 mg/kg every six hours, a reversible reduction in fibula growth rate has been observed upon discontinuation of the drug. Animal studies have demonstrated that tetracyclines cross the placenta, accumulate in fetal tissues, and may exert toxic effects on the developing fetus, including skeletal development retardation. Embryotoxicity has also been observed in animal studies when tetracyclines were administered early in pregnancy. If tetracycline is used during pregnancy or if a patient becomes pregnant while taking the drug, the patient should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. Tetracycline should only be used during pregnancy if absolutely necessary. In patients with renal impairment, even standard oral or parenteral doses of tetracycline may result in excessive systemic accumulation and potential liver toxicity. In such cases, lower total doses are recommended, and prolonged therapy may necessitate monitoring of serum drug levels. Photosensitivity reactions, characterized by exaggerated sunburn, have been reported in some individuals taking tetracyclines. The antianabolic effects of tetracyclines can lead to elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels. While this is not typically problematic in individuals with normal renal function, patients with significant renal impairment may experience azotemia, hyperphosphatemia, and acidosis due to higher serum tetracycline levels. As with other antibiotics, tetracycline use may result in the overgrowth of nonsusceptible organisms, including fungi. If superinfection occurs, the drug should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. Infections caused by Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci should be treated for a minimum of ten days. Bulging fontanels in infants and benign intracranial hypertension in adults have been reported in association with tetracycline use, both of which resolved upon discontinuation of the drug. When indicated, surgical interventions such as incision and drainage should be performed alongside antibiotic therapy. Tetracycline should not be prescribed in the absence of a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication, as this increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria without providing benefit to the patient. Patients should be counseled that tetracycline and other antibacterial drugs are only effective against bacterial infections and do not treat viral infections, such as the common cold. Patients should be instructed to take the medication exactly as prescribed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. Skipping doses or failing to complete the full course of treatment may reduce the drug's effectiveness and increase the risk of bacterial resistance. In cases of venereal disease where coexistent syphilis is suspected, dark-field examinations should be performed before initiating treatment, and blood serology should be repeated monthly for at least four months. For long-term therapy, periodic laboratory evaluations of organ systems, including hematopoietic, renal, and hepatic function, are recommended. Tetracycline should not be used concurrently with penicillin or other bactericidal antibiotics, as bacteriostatic drugs may interfere with their action. Tetracyclines have been shown to depress plasma prothrombin activity, so patients on anticoagulant therapy may require dose adjustments. Concurrent use of tetracycline and methoxyflurane has been associated with fatal renal toxicity. The absorption of tetracyclines is impaired by antacids containing aluminum, calcium, or magnesium, as well as by preparations containing iron, zinc, or sodium bicarbonate. Additionally, tetracycline may reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives. Long-term animal studies are ongoing to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of tetracycline hydrochloride. Related antibiotics, such as oxytetracycline and minocycline, have shown evidence of oncogenic activity in rats. In in vitro mammalian cell assays, tetracycline hydrochloride demonstrated mutagenicity at concentrations of 60 mcg/mL in mouse lymphoma cells and 10 mcg/mL in Chinese hamster lung cells. However, tetracycline hydrochloride did not affect fertility when administered to male and female rats at doses equivalent to 25 times the human dose. Tetracycline is classified as Pregnancy Category D due to evidence of teratogenic effects (refer to Warnings). Pregnant women with renal disease may be at increased risk of developing tetracycline-associated liver failure. The effects of tetracyclines on labor and delivery are unknown. Nursing mothers should be advised of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants exposed to tetracyclines. A decision should be made to either discontinue the drug or cease nursing, taking into account the importance of the drug to the mother (refer to Warnings). For pediatric use, refer to the Warnings and Dosage and Administration sections.
